clinicalPearls: Conjunctivochalasis is redundant, loose bulbar conjunctiva that folds over the lower lid margin, most prominent in the inferior interpalpebral zone, and is a very common age-related change often mistaken for simple dry eye.

Symptoms are variable and position-dependent: irritation, foreign-body sensation, unstable tear film and either epiphora (when folds obstruct the inferior punctum and tear meniscus) or paradoxical dryness.
The redundant folds disrupt the tear meniscus and are aggravated by blinking and downgaze, so symptoms characteristically worsen on reading and looking down.

Diagnosis is clinical at the slit lamp; asking the patient to blink and look down, and gently pressing the lid against the globe, demonstrates the mobile conjunctival folds interposed between globe and lid.
First-line management is conservative with ocular lubricants and topical anti-inflammatory measures, and treatment of any coexisting dry eye and lid disease.
Surgery (conjunctival resection with primary closure, cautery or amniotic-membrane grafting) is reserved for symptoms refractory to medical therapy.
It frequently coexists with, and is confused for, aqueous-deficient or evaporative dry eye; recognising the redundant folds explains symptoms that persist despite adequate lubrication.
Mechanical chafing from the folds can cause localised conjunctival injection, subconjunctival haemorrhage and, occasionally, epithelial breakdown.
reference.pathophysiology: Age-related degeneration weakens the attachment of the bulbar conjunctiva to the underlying Tenon capsule and sclera, so redundant conjunctiva accumulates and prolapses over the lower lid margin. Elastotic degeneration, increased matrix metalloproteinase activity, chronic mechanical friction between the lid and globe during blinking, and local inflammation with lymphatic dilatation all contribute to loss of elastic tissue and conjunctival laxity. The redundant folds disrupt the tear meniscus and tear distribution, may occlude the inferior punctum causing epiphora, and by delaying tear clearance perpetuate ocular surface inflammation.
additionalDifferentials: Aqueous-deficient or evaporative dry eye disease
Punctal or nasolacrimal duct obstruction causing epiphora
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp assessment of conjunctival folds in primary gaze, downgaze and on blinking
Tear film evaluation with break-up time and ocular surface staining
Fluorescein clearance / tear meniscus assessment to demonstrate impaired tear drainage
Lissamine green staining of redundant folds
Assessment of lid position and punctal patency to distinguish other causes of epiphora
Anterior-segment photography to document extent and monitor progression
redFlags: Persistent unilateral redundancy or a mass-like fold that could represent conjunctival neoplasia
Progressive epiphora with signs of nasolacrimal obstruction requiring lacrimal evaluation
Corneal epithelial breakdown or dellen from chronic mechanical exposure
Symptoms disproportionate to findings prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: A benign, chronic degenerative condition; most patients are controlled with lubricants and conservative measures. Surgical correction of symptomatic cases generally gives good and durable symptomatic relief.
pitfalls: Labelling the patient as pure dry eye and escalating lubricants while missing the mechanical role of the redundant folds
Attributing epiphora solely to lacrimal obstruction and performing unnecessary lacrimal surgery
Failing to examine in downgaze and on blinking, so the folds are not appreciated
Overlooking coexisting lid malposition or dry eye that must be treated concurrently
Proceeding to surgery before an adequate trial of medical therapy
